Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us recite (pp.70–71): teacher-led read-aloud then choral recitation of the poem.

periods.activity_title: Meeting the Poem: Read-Aloud and Choral Recitation

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the full poem aloud twice with expressive voice, pausing at each 'Oh! What a BIG…' to let wonder register. Students listen with books open at pages 70–71.
Let us recite — teacher models one stanza at a time; class echoes chorally. Repeat until all four stanzas flow with natural rhythm and volume on 'BIG' and 'SPLISH-SPLASH'.
Paired recitation: students take turns reading one stanza each to a partner, coaching each other on expression. Teacher circulates and offers quiet encouragement.
Whole-class recitation from memory of the final two stanzas; teacher prompts with the first word of each line if needed.
Teacher asks one or two volunteers to name their favourite line and say what picture it made in their mind. Brief, unhurried sharing to close.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's anaphoric structure ('If all the … were one …') is its greatest gift for choral work — each stanza is nearly identical in shape, so students gain confidence quickly. Watch for 'SPLISH-SPLASH': encourage full voice and a hand-clap on the two syllables rather than a shy mumble. Books should stay open throughout; this is a first encounter, not a test of memory.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us recite (pp.70–71): repeated reading for fluency followed by guided discussion of the poem's imaginative structure.

periods.activity_title: Reading Deeper: Comprehension Discussion and Repeated Reading

time_bands.activity: Having chanted the poem together, open with a quick paired chant of the whole poem at pages 70–71 to warm up voices and remind students of the full shape.

Teacher leads a comprehension discussion: 'What does the poet imagine about laddoos? About children? About the sea?' Students respond in sentences; teacher weaves answers into a simple retelling of the poem's logic.

Guided close-reading of the final two stanzas: teacher asks 'What happens when the BIG child picks the BIG Laddoo?' and 'What sound does it make?' Students locate lines and read them aloud, discussing why SPLISH-SPLASH is written in capitals.
Students do an independent repeated reading of the whole poem silently, then one volunteer reads it aloud to the class for fluency. Teacher gives brief, warm feedback on expression.
Teacher poses a closing wondering question — 'What would YOU throw into a big sea?' — for students to think about quietly. No written answer needed.

periods.teacher_notes: Having chanted the poem in its entirety, students are ready to look at why the poem works — the repeating pattern and the surprise at the end. The onomatopoeic 'SPLISH-SPLASH' is a natural anchor for discussing how sound words create delight; do not rush past it. Students who are unsure of comprehension questions can always return to the text — keep books open throughout.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think (p.72): guided conversation about big laddoos, big foods, and varieties of laddoos.
Let us speak (p.73): role-play Meena explaining how she knew the sweet was a laddoo.

periods.activity_title: Talking About Laddoos and Big Things: Guided Conversation

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to recall the poem's giant laddoo and asks: 'Have you ever seen or eaten a really big laddoo?' Students share briefly with a partner to warm up.

Let us think — teacher facilitates a guided conversation around all three prompts at page 72: big laddoos students have seen, other very big foods, and different kinds of laddoos. Teacher models complete sentences and encourages students to do the same.

Let us speak — teacher reads the story of Jithu and Meena aloud (page 73, picture on the same page). Students look at the picture, then think in pairs: 'What did Meena say when Jithu asked how she knew?' Pairs share their ideas with the class.

Teacher leads a brief class discussion: 'Which sense did Meena use?' Students name touch, smell, and shape as possible clues. A few volunteers demonstrate by closing their eyes and describing an imaginary object.
Closing: one or two students share the most interesting laddoo variety they mentioned. Teacher affirms the range with a brief, warm comment.

periods.teacher_notes: The Jithu-and-Meena story is a gentle entry point into senses and empathy — Meena cannot see, so she uses touch and perhaps smell. Students may give many different answers for what Meena said, and all reasonable ones deserve affirmation. Keep the conversation moving; the goal is confident speaking in full sentences, not a single correct answer.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think (p.72): sort round things into 'can be eaten' and 'cannot be eaten' columns.
Let us think (p.72): write what happened to the Big Laddoo after it splashed into the sea.

periods.activity_title: Writing About Shapes, Imagination, and Festivals

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a large two-column table on the board labelled 'That can be eaten' and 'That cannot be eaten' and asks students to call out round things they know. Teacher records three examples to model.

Let us think — students open textbooks to page 72 and independently complete the two-column sorting task in their notebooks, writing at least three items in each column. Teacher circulates and prompts: 'Is a football round? Can you eat it?'

Let us think — teacher reads aloud the poem's final image (the giant laddoo hitting the giant sea) and asks: 'What do you think happened to the laddoo after the SPLISH-SPLASH?' Students draft one or two sentences in their notebooks. Teacher models a sample sentence on the board before students write.
Three or four volunteers read their laddoo-in-the-sea sentences aloud. Class responds with a thumbs-up for any vivid or surprising idea. Teacher highlights variety of imagination.
Teacher sets homework: at page 77, students write the name of their favourite festival and three sweets or dishes made on that day. Teacher reads the prompt aloud so it is clear.

periods.teacher_notes: The sorting task (round things, edible or not) connects the poem's central image to everyday observation — both thinking and vocabulary are exercised. For the imaginative sentence about the laddoo in the sea, accept any plausible or playful answer; dissolving, floating, being eaten by fish, and growing even bigger are all valid and worth celebrating. The festival-food homework taps personal knowledge, so every student will have something to write.

homework.task_brief: Let us write (p.77): write your favourite festival and the sweets or dishes made on that day.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write A (p.74): frame sentences using consonant-cluster words — play, plum, cloud, clock, blue, blanket.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the six words on the board (play, plum, cloud, clock, blue, blanket) and reads each aloud, asking students to repeat and notice the two-consonant start. Teacher models: 'I play cricket every evening.' Students copy the model into notebooks.

Let us write A — students open to page 74. Teacher models a sentence for 'plum' ('A ripe plum is sweet and purple.'), then guides students to draft their own sentences for 'cloud' and 'clock' together as a class before they work independently on the remaining words.

Students write their own sentences for all six words in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, giving brief verbal feedback — pointing out capital letters, full stops, and whether the sentence makes sense.
Volunteers share one sentence each for different words. Class listens and the teacher highlights a strength in each sentence (interesting detail, correct punctuation, vivid image) before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored the poem's playful language, students now practise the consonant clusters (pl, cl, bl) that appear in the textbook's word-building section. Modelling before independent writing is essential — show what a complete, interesting sentence looks like, not just a grammatically minimal one. Students who finish early may try using two of the words in a single sentence.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.73): brainstorm and write words that describe a laddoo.
Let us write B (p.74): match male animals to their female counterparts.

periods.activity_title: Describing Words and Animal Pairs: Word Games

time_bands.activity: Let us learn — teacher asks: 'If you had to describe a laddoo to someone who has never seen one, what words would you use?' Students call out words; teacher writes them on the board (round, sweet, yellow, big, soft, crumbly). Class discusses which words describe how it looks, feels, tastes, and smells.

Students copy the best describing words into their notebooks with a small sketch of a laddoo, labelling it with at least four words from the board. Teacher reinforces: these are words that tell us more about a thing.

Let us write B — teacher writes the six male animal names on the board and reads them aloud (cock, lion, peacock, mare, bull, drake). Students open to page 74. Teacher explains the game: each animal name on the left has a female partner hidden on the right. Students work in pairs to match them in their notebooks.

Teacher takes answers from pairs and writes correct matches on the board. For any disagreement (e.g. mare–horse), teacher explains clearly: a mare IS a horse — the female horse. Students correct their work and read each pair aloud together.
Quick closing chant: teacher calls a male animal name, class calls the female partner in unison. Rapid-fire round with all six pairs to cement the vocabulary.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may notice that 'mare' is already a female animal name and 'horse' is the paired answer — address this directly and warmly, as it is a sharp observation. The describing-words task is grounded in the poem's laddoo imagery, so it connects naturally to what students have already imagined. Avoid telling students these are 'adjectives' as a label until they have felt how the words work.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore A (p.75): test seven objects in water, record which float and which sink.

periods.activity_title: Float or Sink? Hands-On Water Exploration
materials: Objects: piece of paper, small stone, green leaf, pencil, eraser, feather, spoon

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the poem's final image — the giant laddoo thrown into the giant sea — and asks: 'What do you think happened? Did the laddoo float or sink?' Students predict briefly; teacher notes that today the class will test real objects in water.

Teacher displays or names each of the seven objects from page 75 (piece of paper, small stone, green leaf, pencil, eraser, feather, spoon). Students look at the textbook pictures and write their prediction (float or sink) for each object before testing.

Let us explore A — groups of four gather around a tub of water. Each group places objects one by one into the water, observes carefully, and records results in textbook page 75 with ticks for float and crosses for sink.

Class comes back together. Teacher asks each group to share one surprising result. Discussion: 'Did anything float that you thought would sink? Why might a feather float?' Teacher guides without giving the scientific explanation fully — wonder is the goal.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks about the most surprising result they found. Teacher collects or reviews briefly as a record of the exploration.

periods.teacher_notes: The float-and-sink activity grows naturally from the poem's final splash — students have imagined a giant laddoo hitting a giant sea, and now they investigate what actually happens to objects in water. Ensure each group has a shallow tub and a set of objects ready before the sitting begins; the activity window is not long enough to source materials mid-class. Prediction before testing is important — it makes the experiment honest and the surprise real.

periods.activity_title: The Big Laddoo — A Chapter Celebration

time_bands.activity: Whole-class recitation of 'The Big Laddoo' from memory or with books open; children take turns leading a stanza as the rest join in on the 'Oh! What a BIG…' response.

Quick-fire word round: teacher calls out a male animal name (cock, lion, peacock, bull, drake) and groups race to answer with the female counterpart; teacher then calls out a blend word (play, cloud, blanket) and groups say it in a sentence.

Each child writes two or three sentences in their book: 'The poem is about… The part I liked best was… It made me think of…'; teacher circulates and reads quickly, offering a word or two of encouragement.
Children invent one new stanza in the poem's pattern — 'If all the ___ were one ___…' — and share it aloud; class responds with the 'Oh! What a BIG…' chorus together after each.

Teacher draws the chapter together: the poem celebrated the joy of imagining something impossibly huge, from laddoos to seas. Children give a final rousing choral read of the last stanza before the close.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on everything the chapter explored — the poem's cumulative structure, describing words, animal name pairs, the blend words, and the float-or-sink curiosity — without requiring any specific earlier activity to have taken place. Children who encounter this as their first sitting can still participate fully in every band.

items.source_lo: Student reads aloud with expression and discusses the imaginative structure of a cumulative poem using a fantasy poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Cumulative anaphoric poem; gigantism fantasy; onomatopoeia 'SPLISH-SPLASH'; three stanzas plus climax.
items.item_stem: Read the stanza on page 70 beginning "If all the laddoos were one Laddoo". What does the poet imagine in this stanza?

options.label: A
options.text: A child eating many laddoos one by one.

options.label: B
options.text: A child making laddoos in a big kitchen.

options.label: D
options.text: All laddoos joining together to become one enormous laddoo.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be thinking of ordinary eating rather than the poem's imaginative collapsing of all laddoos into one.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused the sea image (from the second and third stanzas) with the laddoo image in the first stanza.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not followed the poem's 'what if' logic and is anchoring to a real-world scenario instead.

items.source_lo: Student reads aloud with expression and discusses the imaginative structure of a cumulative poem using a fantasy poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Cumulative anaphoric poem; gigantism fantasy; onomatopoeia 'SPLISH-SPLASH'; three stanzas plus climax.
items.item_stem: The poem ends with a giant child throwing a giant laddoo into a giant sea and making a 'SPLISH-SPLASH'. Why do you think the poet chose to end the poem with a sound word? What does it add to the poem?

expected_elements: Links it to the fun or surprise of the ending.
Says it helps imagine the big splash.

items.source_context: Personal experience with big foods and laddoo varieties; Meena identifies laddoo by touch/smell despite limited sight.
items.item_stem: Meena cannot see properly, yet she picked up the laddoo from the box of mixed sweets and said 'I love laddoos!' Which of the following best explains how Meena knew it was a laddoo?

options.label: A
options.text: Jithu told her which sweet to pick.

options.label: B
options.text: She felt its round shape and recognised it by touch.

options.label: C
options.text: She read the label on the sweet box.

options.label: D
options.text: She saw the colour of the laddoo clearly.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has not registered that Meena cannot see and is using a sighted strategy.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have missed that Jithu was surprised — he did not guide her choice.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has overlooked the key detail that Meena cannot see properly.

Gives a reason linked to the laddoo's features.

items.item_stem: Before testing in water, predict whether each object will float or sink. Write 'Float' or 'Sink' next to each object.
items.visual_stimulus:
Object | My prediction
a piece of paper | _______________
a small stone | _______________
a green leaf | _______________
a pencil | _______________
an eraser | _______________
a feather | _______________
a spoon | _______________

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Typical results: paper — float (initially), stone — sink, leaf — float, pencil — float, eraser — sink, feather — float, spoon — sink. Accept any reasoned prediction; the value is in comparing prediction to result.

items.item_stem: After you tested the objects in water, share your findings. Tell the class: which object surprised you most — did it float when you thought it would sink, or sink when you thought it would float? Say two sentences about what you found.

expected_elements: Names the surprising object from the experiment.
States their original prediction for that object.
